To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adhesive interactions and friction load relationships have been investigated for nanometre-scale hydrogen bonding monolayers in liquid mixtures of acetone and heptane.

the frictional force of a probe sliding on a surface is the sum of an adhesive and a shear term, that the adhesive term is proportional to the surface shear strength (the free energy of interaction) and that the shear term is proportional to a load-dependent term representing molecular ploughing.

the frictional behaviour of hydrogen-bonded monolayers can be rationalized using DMT mechanics and that the shear term in the frictional response of these monolayers correlates with the free energy change associated with the hydrogen bond formation.

the development of a fundamental understanding of the mechanics of molecular contacts.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanics of molecular contacts are complex and depend on the nature of the interactions, the surface density and the solvent environment.
molecular contacts are governed by a complex combination of adhesion, shear and conformational disruption effects.
the friction force between a surface and a tip can be predicted with high accuracy by a combination of thermodynamic and mechanical models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the friction-load relationship for a molecularly smooth contact in liquids is non-linear, and that the non-linear behaviour can be rationalized in terms of a load-dependent ploughing term and a shear force arising from adhesive interactions.
friction is a function of the free energy of surface interaction, the adhesion force (or surface shear strength) and the load.
the friction-load relationship is a complex combination of the surface chemistry and the liquid environment, and that a simple model such as DMT can only be used as a guide to the underlying physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
molecular friction is a thermodynamic property and can be used to predict molecular interactions.
molecular interactions can be used to tune the friction-load relationship and that the mechanics of frictional interactions can be used as a probe of the thermodynamics of molecular adhesion.
the frictional response of a molecularly smooth surface depends on the adhesion force, and that the friction-load relationship is a sensitive measure of the adhesive interactions.
